summary: GNAP is a protocol for delegating authorization to software. This RFC extends it with ways for resource servers, the services that hold protected data, to connect with authorization servers. It defines how a resource server and its authorization server interact.

plainLanguage.summary: A guard at a door needs a way to ask the ticket office whether a visitor's ticket is real. This defines how the guard and the office talk to each other.

questions: how does a resource server talk to a gnap authorization server
what is the gnap rs-facing api
how does an rs derive a downstream token in gnap
subtitle: How a GNAP authorization server and the resource servers it protects can talk to each other about access tokens.

tldr.problem: Core GNAP does not say how a resource server finds out whether an access token is still valid or what rights it carries, which matters when the authorization server and resource server are run separately.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a common access token model plus an optional resource-server-facing API on the authorization server: discovery, token introspection, resource set registration and a way to derive a downstream token.
tldr.outcome: Authorization servers and resource servers from different operators can interoperate. It is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted.

today: RFC 9767 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2025, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It extends the core protocol in RFC 9635.

sections.title: Why Resource Servers Need an API
sections.content:
The core GNAP specification (RFC 9635) defines two roles: the authorization server (AS), which issues access tokens, and the resource server (RS), which holds the protected data. What it does not define is how the RS gets answers to basic questions, such as whether a given access token is still valid or which access rights it was approved for.

An AS and RS can be one tightly coupled deployment with shared storage, but GNAP does not require that. It is increasingly common for them to be run separately, especially when one AS protects several RSs. RFC 9767 therefore adds three things: a set of optional RS-facing APIs on the AS, a general-purpose access token model, and a method for an RS to derive a downstream token for calling another RS.

How the AS gives a token to the client instance, and how the client presents it to the RS, stay with the core specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket office and the guard often work in different buildings. This RFC gives them a shared language so the guard can check tickets without guessing.

sections.title: The General-Purpose Access Token Model
sections.content:
The client never looks inside an access token, so core GNAP defines no token model. The AS and RS do need one, so this RFC offers a list of aspects that tokens commonly have. It is guidance, not a complete or universal list, and the data can travel in a structured token, in an introspection response, or in both. Where possible each item is mapped to a JSON Web Token claim.

  • Value: the string sent on the wire. It must be unique within a security domain, and the AS chooses it.
  • Issuer (iss) and audience (aud): which AS issued it and which RSs may accept it.
  • Key binding (cnf in a JWT, key in introspection): the key the token is bound to, with its proofing mechanism, unless the token is a bearer token.
  • Access rights (access), flags, and the time validity window (exp, iat, nbf).
  • Token identifier (jti), the authorizing resource owner (sub), the end user, the client instance (client_id in a JWT, instance_id in introspection), a label, and the parent grant request.

Tokens used for the AS's own APIs (continuation, token management, and the RS management token) are called AS-specific access tokens. The AS MUST keep them separate from tokens meant for RSs, any RS attempt to process one MUST fail, and introspection MUST NOT return active true for them.

Token formats can be negotiated at runtime. The AS can list its supported formats in discovery, an RS can require one when registering resources, and the AS can report the format in an introspection response. Every listed format MUST be in the new GNAP Token Formats registry, whose initial entries are jwt-signed, jwt-encrypted, macaroon, biscuit and zcap.
sections.plainLanguage: A ticket can say who gave it out, where it works, what it lets you do and when it runs out. This part is a checklist of those things so everyone describes tickets the same way.

sections.title: Discovery and Protecting RS Requests
sections.content:
An AS offering these services can publish a JSON discovery document at /.well-known/gnap-as-rs, on the same scheme and authority as its grant request endpoint. Its fields are grant_request_endpoint (required), introspection_endpoint, token_formats_supported, resource_registration_endpoint and key_proofs_supported. A missing endpoint means the AS does not offer that feature. Endpoint URLs MUST use https.

Unless otherwise specified, an RS MUST protect its calls to the AS with one of the signature methods from core GNAP. It can present its key by value in a resource_server field or refer to itself by an instance identifier. How the AS learns an RS's keys is out of scope: the AS MAY require preregistration or allow trust on first use.

The AS MAY also issue resource server management access tokens to protect these endpoints. If it does, the RS MUST present them together with its own authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard has to prove who they are before the office will answer. The office may also hand the guard a special badge for the phone line.

sections.title: Token Introspection
sections.content:
With introspection, the RS asks the AS whether a token was issued by it, is valid now, has not been revoked, and suits the RS making the call. The RS signs the request with its own key, not the client's or the token's, and sends a JSON body with access_token (required), proof (recommended), resource_server (required) and optionally access, the minimum rights needed.

An active token was issued by this AS, has not been revoked or expired, is bound using the stated proof method, and is appropriate for the identified RS and the access asked for. If the AS cannot process part of the request, it MUST NOT report the token as active.

The response always has a boolean active. If false, no other fields are returned. If true, it includes access, key (omitted for bearer tokens), iss, and optionally flags, exp, iat, nbf, aud, sub and instance_id. The access array can be filtered for the RS, even to empty. The response MUST NOT include the token value itself. What the RS does next is its own decision.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard phones the office and says: is this ticket real, and what can the holder do? The office answers yes or no, and if yes, tells the guard only what the guard needs to know.

sections.title: Registering Resources and Error Responses
sections.content:
An RS can post the resources it protects to the AS's resource registration endpoint. The request carries access (the rights, in the core GNAP format) and resource_server, and optionally token_formats_supported and token_introspection_required. If the AS cannot honor a requested format or introspection need, it MUST return an error. The RS MUST sign this request with its own key.

The AS replies with a resource_reference, a string standing for the registered list, and optionally an instance_id for later calls and an introspection_endpoint. A client instance can then use that reference as a string-type access right in its own grant request, alongside other rights. If registration fails, the AS returns HTTP 400.

All RS-facing errors use HTTP 400 and a JSON object with an error field, either a code string or an object with code and an optional description. Three codes are defined, and more can be added to a new registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard can also tell the office what rooms they protect. The office gives back a short code for that list, and visitors can ask for it by code.

sections.title: Deriving a Downstream Token
sections.content:
Sometimes an RS must call a second RS to serve a request. The first RS did not make the original grant request, so it cannot change that grant. It needs a new token of its own for the second RS, issued in the context of the incoming token.

Some token formats, such as Macaroons and Biscuits, let the RS derive sub-tokens itself. Otherwise the RS acts as a client instance toward the AS: it uses the same grant endpoint, request and response structures, puts the incoming token in the existing_access_token field, identifies itself with its own key in the client field, and signs the request. The AS MUST check that the presented token is appropriate for the RS making the request. The second RS can repeat the process for further RSs.
sections.plainLanguage: If the guard needs something from another building, they ask the office for a new pass that works only there, instead of lending out the visitor's ticket.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA registered the gnap-as-rs well-known URI suffix and added existing_access_token to the GNAP Grant Request Parameters registry. It also created new registries for token formats, introspection request and response fields, resource set registration request and response parameters, RS-facing discovery document fields, and RS-facing error codes. The error codes are invalid_request, invalid_resource_server and invalid_access.

The registries let other documents add formats, fields and codes without changing this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a public notebook where new words for the guard-and-office language get written down, so nobody invents the same word twice.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
All requests over untrusted networks, from clients to the RS and from the RS to the AS, have to use TLS. The RS must validate the token itself (audience, issuer, subject, the correct key). Validating only the key proof is not enough, since a compromised key or a confused deputy could then make calls beyond what the resource owner authorized. Key proofs must be checked on every request and never cached.

  • Caching: caching validation results helps performance but lets an attacker use a revoked token until the cache expires. A proactive revocation signal to the RS is outside this RFC.
  • Token reuse: an RS holding a bearer token or the key material could reuse the token, so it is safer to exchange it for a contextual token (Section 4). Symmetric keys suit only RSs that are fully trusted.
  • Oversharing: each RS should learn only what it needs, for example through a limited introspection reply.
  • Resource references: the AS should use only fully random or encrypted values so they do not leak internal structure.
  • Privacy: tokens can carry personal information, and introspection tells the AS which RS a token is used at and when.
sections.plainLanguage: Never lend out someone's ticket, check every ticket every time, and only tell each guard what they truly need to know.

items.desc: Missing a required parameter, has an invalid value, or is otherwise malformed.

items.desc: The RS was not recognized or allowed by the AS, or its signature validation failed.

items.desc: The RS may not register or introspect for the requested access value.
